blogs.title: The Normal CT That Wasn't: Re-reviewing Old Imaging When Symptoms Persist
blogs.description: A 14-year-old head CT performed after minor trauma was reported as normal, yet re-review revealed a crowded foramen magnum with loss of CSF space at the craniocervical junction—the earliest clue to Chiari malformation type I. This post explores what a crowded foramen magnum looks like on non-contrast CT, why this finding is easily missed in the context of trauma imaging, and when persistent unexplained symptoms should prompt clinicians to pull old studies and look again. The case serves as a powerful reminder of how anchoring bias and satisfaction of search in radiology interpretation can delay diagnosis for over a decade.

blogs.title: Seven Years, Five Scopes, Zero Answers: When Normal Endoscopy Means Think Neurologically
blogs.description: This patient underwent three laryngoscopies and two upper GI endoscopies over seven years—all normal—before anyone considered a neurological cause for her choking. The post dissects the clinical reasoning that should have triggered an earlier pivot: difficulty with solids AND liquids equally is a hallmark of neurogenic, not mechanical, dysphagia. We review the evidence that CMI is over-represented in patients with persistent unexplained dysphagia, discuss lower cranial nerve compression patterns in Chiari, and offer a practical framework for when to stop scoping and start imaging the brainstem.

blogs.title: Forgetting to Breathe: The Dissociation of Voluntary and Automatic Ventilation in Brainstem Compression
blogs.description: This patient's oxygen saturation dropped to 70–80% without any sensation of dyspnea—at an airport, she was found at 78% SpO2 and felt only dizzy. This post explores the remarkable pathophysiology of central hypoventilation in CMI, where voluntary breathing remains intact but automatic brainstem-mediated respiratory drive fails during sleep or distraction. We examine how tonsillar compression disrupts medullary respiratory centers and afferent pathways to the cortex, explaining the dangerous absence of air hunger. The 'Ondine's curse' phenotype, its distinction from congenital PHOX2B-related central hypoventilation, and the clinical implications of patients who literally forget to breathe are discussed.

blogs.title: AHI of 6.0 but Sats of 70%: How Your Sleep Study Can Underestimate Central Hypoventilation
blogs.description: Despite documented oxygen desaturations to 70–80%, this patient's type III sleep study showed only a mildly elevated AHI of 6.0. This post unpacks the critical methodological limitation: without EEG, AHI is calculated using total recording time rather than true sleep time, potentially underestimating event frequency by including wakeful periods. We discuss when type III studies are insufficient, when to escalate to type I polysomnography with full EEG and capnography, and how to reconcile discrepant clinical and polysomnographic data when the clinical picture strongly suggests central hypoventilation.

blogs.title: The Weight of Her Hair: Scalp Allodynia, Vertex Pain, and Chiari Malformation
blogs.description: Fourteen years of occipital and vertex headaches with marked allodynia so severe that the weight of her own hair triggered pain led this patient to cut her hair short—against cultural norms—reducing baseline pain from 6/10 to 3/10. This post explores the underrecognized headache phenotypes associated with CMI, including occipital neuralgia, the recently described 'burning vertex syndrome,' and nummular headache. We discuss the proposed small-fibre pathway mechanisms, the absence of validated symptom assessment tools for CMI headache patterns, and the cultural and quality-of-life dimensions of symptomatic management decisions.

blogs.title: Watchful Waiting or Posterior Fossa Decompression: Managing Symptomatic Chiari with Central Apnea
blogs.description: This patient chose conservative management with quarterly overnight oximetry and annual MRI surveillance despite having 11 mm tonsillar descent, predominantly central sleep apnea, and documented life-threatening desaturations. This post examines the clinical decision-making framework for CMI patients with respiratory manifestations, reviewing evidence that posterior fossa decompression can restore CSF flow dynamics and reverse respiratory symptoms, indications for surgery versus observation, the role of multidisciplinary consultation, and practical guidance on structuring a monitoring plan for patients who defer surgery.
